issues.title: Thomas Fossati ' comments
issues.author: junzhanghw
issues.body:
Achieved from 
https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/agent2agent/SUGlc6vgg5CoViVh1dkk8c6PiOU/

1. Many of the challenges described (cross-domain visibility, delegation
chains, evolving authorisation) apply to *any* complex distributed
microservice architecture.  Unsure of what makes this problem strictly
unique to AI agents?  Could this work be generalised to something like
"dynamic workload delegation" without the AI buzzword? :-)

2. There seems to be quite a lot of overlap with WIMSE, OAUTH, SCITT,
RATS -- at least, which is both good and bad.  To minimise the risk of
overlap, conflict, et cetera, I suggest you make the proposal visibile
to these groups (if you haven't already done it).  I understand it may
be a bit too early to properly engage, but a quick heads-up would not
hurt (_maybe_).

3. It is not entirely clear to me how does this work would differ from
existing distributed tracing standards, e.g., OpenTelemetry / W3C Trace
Context?  Is the goal to add cryptographic proof to traces, or to define
an entirely new transport mechanism?

4. The charter proposes linking user-facing interactions (the prompts)
with system-facing interactions (the API calls) across domains.  How is
the architecture going to handle the mega privacy implications of
transmitting user prompts / intent across administrative boundaries?

5. What is the threat model for the audit data itself?  I may be missing
something but I don't get how we can ensure that a compromised agent
cannot forge/alter/drop its own audit trails before they are recorded?

6. The charter mentions that AI agent behavior may be non-deterministic.
If an agent hallucinates a step or takes an odd path, is the intention
to standardise a data model that can also capture "why" an agent did
something, rather than just "what" it did?

7. The chapter mentiones the need to distinguish between user, agent,
and service identities.  I hope this doesn't require new identity
primitives and instead leverages existing ones like SPIFFE IDs, DIDs &
co.  It'd help if this was made more explitic.

8. I am especially ignorant in this space, so it's a bit unclear to me
what the target audience is for this audit data?  Is it for end-users to
see what an agent did on their behalf, for compliance folks to audit an
organisation, or for downstream APIs to decide whether to authorise an
action?  Or all of the the above?  I guess tHe answer to this may have a
major impact on the data model.

8. Have major AI framework developers expressed interest in implementing
any interoperable standards that would come out of this pipeline?

comments.author: junzhanghw
comments.body:
comments from Thomas Howe
https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/agent2agent/gfVRfv94g-eTtH9qZOlzxUCEVd0/

(At least) one of your questions lands straight into the VCON working group:

> 
> The charter proposes linking user-facing interactions (the prompts) with
> system-facing interactions (the API calls) across domains. How is the
> architecture going to handle the mega privacy implications of transmitting
> user prompts / intent across administrative boundaries?
> 
> 

VCONs have a really neat facility in that you can take an original, create a data-reduced version of it to share, that points back to the original. ( https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-02.html#redacted-object ) All of that can be recorded in SCITT.  So,  you can control the information that crosses security boundaries without losing provenance, integrity and data subject consent.

Also, there's an answer for

> 
> "What is the threat model for the audit data itself? I may be missing
> something but I don't get how we can ensure that a compromised agent
> cannot forge/alter/drop its own audit trails before they are recorded?"
> 
> 
> 
> 

You are not missing anything, and a compromised agent absolutely can lie about its own records. The architecture starts from "the Agent is not trusted" (Section 8). Defence against forgery/omission comes from three independent sources:

* the service the agent calls produces its own corroborating record on its side of the wire,

* consequential actions are registered with a transparency service, so omission and equivocation become detectable across relying parties, and

* RATS attestation can bind records to a known execution environment, raising the bar for silent tampering.

None of these layers alone is sufficient; combined, they let a relying party or auditor detect inconsistencies even when the agent's audit store is fully under the attacker's control. A proper threat model is one of the things the WG should produce.

issues.title: Michael Richardson‘s comments
issues.author: junzhanghw
issues.body:
Achieved from
https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/agent2agent/ZX6mUUD8htUCyOFt7OfnD0-KKPw/


1. Terminology & Naming

- On the term "AI":

"AI" is a decade specific marketing term, and has negative technical content. It used to mean "plays chess", then it meant "Expert System", and then... What we have today are machine learning systems based upon LLM. Please say so once, and then use the term "Agent" in the rest of the charter.

- On the acronym "AUDIT":

I am, however, concerned that the TLA AUDIT, does not on its own convey much without knowing its expansion. Pass that TLA through a few layers of PHB, and too much context is lost, and it can mean all sorts of things way out of our scope.

- Proposal for a new name:

maybe something like: AGENTIC = AGent Engagement with Non-repudable Traceable In Cross-domain

2. Architecture Document Details

- On the diagram label:

("Attestation" alone in a diagram that Henk wrote? Surely, that should be "Attestation Results"?)

- On Section 7 (JSON Example):

I like that section 7 is trying to provide an Illustration of an EXAMPLE, but perhaps the use of what looks like very concrete JSON will confuse some. Is there a way to be slightly less detailed here?

3. Granular Authorization Complexity

- On the need for detailed permissions:

On the whole, I think that Agentic uses are going to force most resource providers to create many low-level detailed permissions that can be seperately delegatable. It's not enough to just split out every day operations from accounting/data affecting ones. Many of the every day operations will need to be split into multiple authorizations.

- On historical failures (VMS/NTFS):

Many systems have a primitive two-level view... There is a long history of the challenges of very detailed permissions problems. VMS and NTFS have quite detailed lists of permissions, and it was often difficult for administrators to know exactly what permissions were needed for a particular operation. After three iterations with the admin trying to figure things out, the admin would often just throw every possible permission at the user in frustration.

- On the risk of "Overly specific" vs "too coarse":

Overly specific and too coarse permissions/authorizations are a problem. We continue to see some of this legacy in some of the local priviledge escalation attacks against core desktop security tools like MS-Defender: it has privileges beyond what one would think it needs because it has to get around somethings else.

4. Standardization of Authorization Description

- Critique of OAuth2 approach:

OAUTH2 has, wisely I think, punted on the problem of what is being authorized to the resource owner. This made sense at the time, although I think it has put too much power into a few resource owners. I do not think that it will be effective for this WG to do the same.

- The "Rabbit Hole" warning:

At the time, we also can't go down the rabbit hole of trying to define an entire ontology of authorizations required for any particular target (i.e., "booking a hotel room" or seting up a pre-authorized debit for "a municipal tax authority")

- The Proposal (Mechanism for Experts):

What I think that we can do is create a concise process for experts in that domain to describe their authorization ontology. Yes, it will need to be machine readable.

- Challenge to the Charter (Scope):

so I don't know how we can audit delegations of authorizations without having a good way to describe them. Particularly across "ADMINISTRATIVE" boundaries.

Requirement for Relationships:

At least, I think that we need to know if a FINE-GRAINED authorization is part of some other coarse-grained authorization, and we might also have situations where there are multiple coarse-grained authorizations which contain the same FINE-GRAINED authorization.

issues.title: LUCIA CABANILLAS RODRIGUEZ‘s comments
issues.author: junzhanghw
issues.body:
achieved from 
https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/agent2agent/ucCt6vdc2v_RN53Ylbkq2BiAn4k/


1. On making policy evolution a first-class auditable object:

"One aspect that may deserve additional emphasis is making policy evolution and authorization provenance first-class auditable objects, not only the resulting actions. In many AI-agent scenarios, understanding why a policy changed, which context or behavioural signals triggered it, and which authority or component approved or derived the change may become as important as auditing the final action itself."

2. On standardizing evidence correlation across trust boundaries:

"I think it could be useful to explicitly consider standardized mechanisms for correlating evidence across domains, especially when delegation chains span multiple trust boundaries with partially shared policies and heterogeneous enforcement models."

3. On ensuring the audit structure supports specific relationships:

"I think there is a strong connection with the need you identify for a common and interoperable audit structure capable of correlating identities, delegation chains, authorization transitions, and causal relationships across domains and over time. The ability to consistently represent trace identifiers, preceding-event relationships, 'on-behalf-of' delegation semantics, authorization scope, validity, and policy provenance becomes critical once agents dynamically derive, transform, and share authorization state during execution."

4. On connecting policy provenance mechanisms to the auditing architecture:

"I think those provenance mechanisms could naturally complement the auditing architecture, particularly for reconstructing how a specific authorization state or decision was reached at a given point in time."

5. On integrating with existing policy sharing models:

"The draft focuses on interoperable representation and distribution of authorization policies across heterogeneous and automated environments using a common YANG-based model. While it already considers accounting aspects, I think it would need further evolution to fully support auditing."

issues.title: toshiyuki sato's comments
issues.author: junzhanghw
issues.body:
achieved from 
https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/agent2agent/_yXD3mlY7PbexK0H-EoMq6Xo7Gs/

The result is that the audit record contains a pre-action statement of
intent that is structurally prior to the action, making ex-post fabrication
of reasoning impossible in a conforming implementation. "Why" is captured
before "what" happens, not reconstructed after.

This is the architectural distinction Chris Hood flagged in this thread —
pre-commitment intent declaration is different in kind from post-hoc audit
recording. The two compose: IDP provides the "why before what" record;
GAR-00 provides the non-suppressible session audit that carries it.

https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-sato-soos-idp/
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-sato-soos-gar/

issues.title: Diego R. Lopez's comments
issues.author: junzhanghw
issues.body:
Achieved from
https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/agent2agent/7ynLOIMhS9KvmsMOpSkq743YK2w/


1) Is there general interest in agent auditing work in the IETF? Are there other people who maybe already work on this topic or a planning to?

I do believe this is rather interesting work though, as Thomas said, I think it would be much more interesting if we refrain from limiting it to the fashionable agents, and it is made clear this would be applicable to any workload (to use the WIMSE terminology) or, if you want to keep the “A” in the proposed name, to any *actor* able to interact with other actors and services in the Internet. Even a broad enough definition of the term “agent” would do...

I am aware this would imply the need of defining the “actor” term, but I think the extra work would be justified by the evident advantages of generality, and also by not tying the fate of this proposal to something that could follow the not-so-glorious path of other past hot topics.

Regarding the second part of the question, we have been working in mechanisms that could be applicable to this idea, such as the draft on YANG data provenance (suitable to be generalized in this context, see https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-opsawg-yang-provenance/) another draft on identity chaining (where the “actor” term is used intentionally, see https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-mw-oauth-actor-chain/) and an open-source approach to evidence collection we had the intention to bring to the IETF soon.

2) Any comments on the proposed scope of the work? Is the scope clear? Is the IETF the right place for this work? Does this need a new working group?

The scope seems clear to me, though I would prefer to make it less “agentical”. In despite of having many potential intersections with other WGs, or even precisely because of this, I believe the proposed work deserves a specific WG.

Regarding the deliverables, I think it could be interesting to make deliverable (1) identify those protocols and models suitable to be considered in the deliverables mentioned in (3), to avoid any future profile creep when trying to address those documents.

And I agree with Lionel that the mention in (1) to only user-facing and system-facing signals seems a little bit limiting, excluding agent/actor chains.

3) Any comments on the proposed architecture or any additional work in the space!

Let me insist in two of my previous comments:


  1.
Make it less “agentical”, with either agents as a relevant (may the most relevant) use case, or a definition of “agent” that is wide enough to accommodate other use cases.
  2.
Consider in the introduction (and the diagram in Figure 1) the idea of a chain of agents/actors

issues.title: WI-4 Action Record Profile: candidate input + worked contract-negotiation use case (ran at IETF 126 hackathon)
issues.author: StevenMih
issues.body:
Opening this to follow up my comments in the session happening right now.  
Great open discussion. Thanks for running it this way.

WI-4 currently names no candidate format (WI-3 names verifiable-agent-conversations
for Interaction Records). Offering the Agent Action Capsule as input for the Action
Record slot, in the same spirit as input only.

Why it matches WI-4's stated bindings:

- Produced at the effect boundary: `effect.status` (planned/dispatched/confirmed/
  failed/reverted) with a MUST-digest over the OBSERVED response for `confirmed` —
  overclaim is a protocol violation, not a convention.

- Bound to the authorizing token: `effect.authorization` carries typed references
  {type, digest_alg, digest} to permits/mandates — the token body never enters the
  record (Delegation-Record privacy by construction).

- Bound to attestation: `effect_attestation` (runtime_claimed | gate_executed), and
  the record's outcome digest has been bound into a RATS TPM quote (AEP composition).

- "Absence of Evidence is itself audit-relevant": refusals, timeouts, and
  countersign-refusals are first-class verdicts (`verdict_class`), not gaps —
  including bilateral/cross-org endings (draft-mih-agent-bilateral-attestation-01).

- SCITT-native: COSE_Sign1 Signed Statement, registered to transparency services;
  relevant to WI-7 as well — this weekend at the IETF 126 hackathon one statement was
  registered on two independent Transparency Services (a CCF instance and an
  RFC9162_SHA256 log) with both receipts verified by independent verifiers.

Worked use case, ran at the 126 hackathon: agent-negotiated contracts.
A buyer agent (identity: an AI-Catalog entry, by digest) discovers multiple seller agents
on a second agent registry (NANDA Index), opens a private room per vendor, and they
negotiate autonomously — offers, counters, trades. One consequential act closes
it: buyer accepts, seller countersigns, both hold a byte-identical sealed record
of the agreed terms, anchored to a public transparency log. Per 126 side meeting BoF Q2, this is the provable side. 

How that run maps to this draft's record types:

- Interaction Record — the negotiation dialogue: recorded and digest-committed,
  disclosed to no one; any line is promotable to provable later if a dispute
  needs it. Per 126 side meeting BoF Q2, this is the recorded side.

- Action Record — the acceptance: the boundary event, provable to a stranger;
  live example still running this week at IETF 126: GET /v1/bindings/{id}/verify on the hackathon demo service returns
  verified:true with the recomputed sealed-terms hash. Here is one such record of the buyer-accepts/seller-countersigns contract record, sealed Saturday, anchored, checkable by anyone : https://accountable-dealroom-1020437450833.us-central1.run.app/v1/bindings/544f9878a449473588b6f424b36fec51/verify

- Delegation Record — each agent acts under its principal's mandate (budget
  ceiling, must-have terms), cited BY DIGEST: the record proves the agent stayed
  inside its authority without the ceiling ever being revealed to the counterparty.

- Authorization Transition — the endings where the other side doesn't play:
  vendor timeout, delivery-unconfirmed, countersign-refused — each a signed,
  anchored, first-class outcome. A contract system that cannot prove "they never
  answered" cannot support a dispute. Getting "ghosted" has meaning. 

The general split this run suggests for Section 5: boundary events and authority
are provable-by-default; deliberation is recorded-and-committed, promotable on
demand.

Running code + evidence: 32 frozen conformance vectors (pos/neg, named failing
stages), Python + clean-room Go verifiers, cross-implementation re-runs by
independent parties at the hackathon. 
Repo: 
github.com/action-state-group/agent-action-capsule 
(vectors pinned at tag `vectors-ietf126`).

issues.title: WI-6 (Profile of RATS Evidence): freshness should bind to the action, and the assumed root of trust should be explicit
issues.author: tyche-dev
issues.body:
Raised briefly at the IETF 126 side meeting this morning; writing it up as promised.

Two findings from an implementation of an action record carrying an attestation result for its executing environment, appraised by an independently-built RATS verifier — a different implementation from the one that produced the evidence, so the appraisal is not self-confirming.

### 1. Freshness is the hard part, and it is an action-level property

The architecture lets a record carry inline Evidence, an Attestation Result, or a stable reference to either. What it does not yet pin down is *what the appraisal is fresh with respect to*.

Binding freshness to the session is the intuitive choice, and I think it is the wrong one. An agent's session may outlive many actions, and the executing environment can change between them. A profile that does not force the appraisal to bind to the individual action admits records that are individually well-formed and jointly misleading — every record verifies, and the sequence still misrepresents what executed what.

This seems worth stating as a requirement in WI-6 rather than leaving it to implementers.

### 2. The architecture currently reads as software-rooted

RATS Evidence, Attestation Results and Endorsements are all reused as the vocabulary for environmental claims, which is the right foundation. But nothing in the document says whether the executing environment's root of trust is expected to be hardware, and that distinction changes what the profile has to carry.

It matters most in exactly the case the problem statement is aimed at. Where the relying party does not trust the agent's operator, a software-rooted appraisal reduces to "the operator says so" — which is the assumption the audit store was introduced to remove. Cross-domain is where that reduction bites.

I am not arguing the profile should mandate hardware roots. I am arguing it should be explicit about which it assumes, because the security properties differ and today a reader cannot tell.

---

Happy to contribute concrete text for WI-6, or evidence samples if that is more useful. I can share the implementation details on request; one of the papers describing it is under blind review at the moment, so I have kept links out of this issue rather than out of any reluctance to show the work.

issues.title: Confidentiality & leakage across the architecture: content, identity, correlation. Suggested text for Section 9 and WI-7
issues.author: StevenMih
issues.body:
Per the 126 side meeting Q3 about confidentiality and info-leakage considerations, proposing to address leakage at 3 different layers, with different mechanisms.

1. CONTENT. Prove bindings without disclosing payloads. Content-addressing plus salted commitments for low-entropy fields: a verifier checks the digest; the subject discloses selectively (the SD-JWT model, RFC 9901, applies per-field to JSON records). This ran cross-org at the 126 hackathon — bindings verified end to end without any invoice contents traveling.

2. IDENTITY. Records should carry role descriptors, not end-user identities. The approver/principal reference belongs in the authorization document the record cites by digest, not in the audit-record body itself. Audit trails that embed natural-person identity inherit data-protection obligations they don't need.

3. CORRELATION. The transparency layer itself leaks. A single TS observing all of an operator's registrations is a traffic-analysis channel (volume, timing, counterparty patterns) even when payloads are digests only. Two multi-TS modes should be distinguished, because they serve opposite goals: MIRRORING the same statement to several logs increases trust-diversity and availability but multiplies observers; 
PARTITIONING different registrations across logs (per counterparty, per context, or rotating) means each log sees only a slice, and correlation requires collusion especially when combined with pseudonymous registration identity. 

Suggest WI-7's registration-policy profile name both modes and their trade-offs, and state what an authorized Auditor may correlate across logs (WI-9) versus what the public may. Cross-TS interop is practical today: at the 126 hackathon one signed statement was verified against receipts from two independent TS (a CCF instance and an RFC9162_SHA256 log) that was mirroring, for trust-diversity; the partitioning mode uses the same machinery.

And one architectural point for Section 9: the record types differ BY CONSTRUCTION in disclosure burden — conversation records carry content and inherit retention/redaction obligations; action records can be content-free entirely. This way deployments can pick the grain that matches their disclosure constraints. I believe its worth a line to describe this feature of the four-type split.

issues.title: Audit references should be content-addressed: a name is not evidence
issues.author: StevenMih
issues.body:
Wherever the architecture carries references: audit context, SC-2/SC-11 tracing identifiers, record-to-record links, we suggest requiring a digest alongside (or as) the identifier. 
Rationale from two incidents in 24 hours at the 126 hackathon: a regenerated evidence bundle under an unchanged filename, and a pinned commit orphaned by a force-push; both caught only by re-hashing, both fixed by naming immutable coordinates. 

Identifiers dangle; digests don't. For an audit architecture, references that can silently change referents are themselves an
integrity hole.

comments.author: LembaGang
comments.body:
Two more data points for this, and one is a different class from the two you name.

Yours are references to artifacts a human placed: a regenerated bundle under an unchanged filename, a commit orphaned by a force-push. Both were caught because a person went back and re-hashed.

The third is a published package version. `@headlessoracle/chirindo@0.3.0` on npm, while the source tree it was cut from was ten commits and an entire feature ahead of it. The test suite was green throughout, because the tests import `src/` and nothing imports `dist/`. Nothing in the repository bound the published artifact to the source tree, so no check could observe the difference.

That matters here because a version string is the identifier a resolver consumes automatically, at install time, with no human looking. A person notices when a documented function is missing. An agent gets `undefined`, routes around it, and reports success on a narrower task. Version numbers are assertions by the publisher, not proofs about contents.

Concretely for the architecture: wherever a record cites a software artifact, a version identifier alone is insufficient for the same reason a filename is. The integrity hash of the distributed artifact is the coordinate that doesn't dangle.

(Note the numbering in this issue predates the SC to WI rename, so the tracing identifiers referenced here are now WI-2 / WI-11.)

issues.title: Composition needs a stated canonicalisation posture per record type: the drafts agree in code, not in text
issues.author: LembaGang
issues.body:
The proposed charter says the working group will "define only the additional protocol elements, data models, and best practices needed to make these compose coherently," and that the aim is to "ensure audit data remains interpretable across systems without shared assumptions." WI-1 (Audit Data Models and Semantics) is where that lands in this draft.

I have been recomputing signed receipt formats across several authors' specifications, byte for byte, and canonicalisation posture is one place where that goal is currently unmet in the text. I want to report it as a documentary gap rather than an interoperability failure, because as far as I can measure the artifacts agree today. What is missing is the normative text that makes the agreement guaranteed rather than observed.

Three postures, across six documents, reading only the published specifications:

- `draft-farley-acta-signed-receipts-02` and `draft-msebenzi-evidence-action-00` name RFC 8785 normatively. **Fixed.**
- `draft-chueayen-attestation-receipts-01` defines its own canonicalisation in Section 5, including rules for number formatting and string encoding. **Own.**
- `draft-borthwick-msebenzi-environment-state-01`, Section 1.2, states that the document does not define "any algorithm for canonicalising signed attestation payloads. Per-type canonicalisation is the responsibility of each type specification." **Delegated.**
- `draft-marques-asqav-compliance-receipts-07` carries the canonicalisation rule per artifact, declared in the Audit Pack manifest entry. **Declared.**

None of these is wrong on its own terms. Delegation and per-artifact declaration are both legitimate designs. The difficulty is only visible when two of them are asked to compose.

The sharpest instance involves a draft I co-author, `draft-borthwick-msebenzi-environment-state-01`. `draft-krausz-verification-state-01`, Section 3.1, states that "the receipt envelope, JCS canonicalization, signed-primitives discipline, and offline-verifiable-against-published-JWKS verification model are identical across the two families," referring to verification.* and environment.*. The environment.* document is the one that declines to define canonicalisation at all. So a cross-family identity is asserted on the one property the other family delegates. A reader cannot check it from the documents, and the draft that creates the gap is mine.

The code is moving while the text stays silent. Two dated instances from `giskard09/argentum-core`, a repository where several of these formats keep conformance fixtures:

- [PR #33](https://github.com/giskard09/argentum-core/pull/33), merged 16 July 2026, re-signed a conformance vector under a strict RFC 8785 verifier. The prior signature had been made over non-strict JCS: the member `skill_results` had been serialised as `status/count/level`, and the strict verifier orders those keys `count/level/status`. Two implementations, one member, different bytes.
- [PR #36](https://github.com/giskard09/argentum-core/pull/36), merged 5 August 2026, introduced a shared `jcs_dumps` helper and applied it to five remaining production sites still calling `json.dumps(sort_keys=True)` directly, which orders by Python code point rather than by UTF-16 code unit as RFC 8785 requires.

The second is worth reading closely. The PR describes itself as a latent-correctness fix, not a live bug fix, and confirms the pinned digests are byte-identical before and after: the documents involved are ASCII-only, so the two orderings coincide. The agreement holds because nothing has yet been serialised outside the Basic Multilingual Plane. That is the shape of the gap. It is not currently producing wrong answers, and nothing in the specifications prevents it from doing so.

I am grateful to Joe Krausz for the PR #36 pointer and for the framing of this as documentary rather than byte-level.

The question for this draft. If audit records are to remain interpretable across systems without shared assumptions, a record type's canonicalisation posture seems to be a property of the record type rather than an implementation detail, and one that has to survive being read by a party holding none of the implementations. Two possibilities, and I do not have a strong view between them:

1. WI-1 requires each record type to state its canonicalisation posture explicitly, with delegation and per-artifact declaration both permitted provided the delegation target or the declaration location is named.
2. The architecture states the composition rule instead: where two record types compose in one audit context, a relying party must be able to determine both postures from published text alone, and it is a defect if it cannot.

The second is weaker and may be enough. Either would have made the instance above visible at review time rather than at recomputation time.

I have no draft to propose for WI-1 and am not asking for one to be adopted. This is a report of something measurable in the current documents, offered because the composition goal is the thing it bears on.

comments.author: LembaGang
comments.body:
**Correction to the `-07` row, prompted by the document's author.**

The issue as filed records `draft-marques-asqav-compliance-receipts-07` as carrying the canonicalisation rule per artifact, declared in the Audit Pack manifest entry. That conflates two layers. Section 4 of `-07` is normative for the receipt layer and inherits the rule itself unchanged:

> The canonicalization rule itself (JCS, [RFC8785]) is inherited unchanged from [ACTA-RECEIPTS]; this section bounds the inputs the rule is applied to.

The bounds are that IEEE-754 floating-point numbers MUST NOT appear in the canonical form covered by a digest, with non-integer values carried as JSON strings or as integer-rational pairs. The per-artifact declarations in the Audit Pack manifest govern digests of *foreign* artifacts referenced by the receipt, such as an `sbom_digest` computed under CycloneDX or SPDX rules, not the receipt's own canonical form.

So `-07` belongs in the **fixed** bucket at the receipt layer, with a per-artifact rule for foreign digests at the reference layer. The survey as filed used four labels: fixed, own, delegated, declared. With this correction the declared label empties at the receipt layer, and the survey reduces to three postures: fixed, own, and delegated. The delegated posture is now represented by exactly one document, `draft-borthwick-msebenzi-environment-state-01`, which I co-author. The sharpest instance in the issue is unchanged.

I am correcting the characterisation by comment rather than editing it out of the body, so the original and this correction both remain visible.

*Edited: an earlier version of this comment said the count was "unchanged at three"; the filed survey used four labels, so the correct statement is that it reduces from four to three. The issue body has also received one clarity edit, naming the co-authored draft at first mention so that draft-krausz-verification-state-01 cannot be read as co-authored; it is sole-authored.*
